analysis.one_liner: Requires phone companies to verify caller IDs and offer free robocall-blocking technology to subscribers.
analysis.headline: A bill to require phone companies to block robocalls died in committee without a vote; the following year a similar measure became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The ROBOCOP Act would have required phone and text providers, at no extra charge, to verify that caller ID information is accurate and to offer subscribers free technology that blocks robocalls and scam calls. Consumers could sue violators for $500 per call, states could sue providers that fail to comply, and the bill would make it illegal to deliberately interfere with call-blocking systems. The FCC would run an appeals and unblocking process so legitimate callers like domestic violence shelters and medical practices are not blocked.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone, but especially older adults and other vulnerable people who are the main targets of phone scams: they would get accurate caller ID and free blocking tools, and a way to recover damages from violators. Legitimate callers who sometimes need masked numbers (domestic violence shelters, medical practices) get an exemption process.

how_it_helps.text: Requires originating providers to verify caller ID at no charge, so scam 'spoofed' numbers stop looking real.

Requires receiving providers to offer free blocking technology that screens out unverified calls and optional technology that blocks calls from autodialers unless the caller is a public safety entity or the subscriber consented.
Lets consumers sue violators for $500 per call (tripled for willful violations) and lets states sue providers with a pattern of failing to offer the technology.
Exempts legitimate users with a need for misleading caller ID, such as domestic violence shelters and medical practices, from the verification mandate.

analysis.who_pays: Phone and text service providers — including big carriers and small phone companies — which would have had to deploy caller-ID verification and call-blocking technology for every subscriber at no extra charge, and face lawsuits of $500 per violation if they failed.

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on phone and text providers, and the bill requires the verification and blocking technology to be offered at no additional charge, so carriers would bear compliance costs that they could otherwise pass to customers or resist as an unfunded mandate.

Aggressive default blocking of unverified calls risks screening out legitimate calls — doctors' offices, schools, delivery services, domestic violence shelters — which the bill tries to manage with an exemption process, a whitelist for essential services, and an appeals process, but the safeguards depend entirely on FCC implementation.
The $500-per-violation private right of action could generate abusive litigation against small providers, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to phone users were large: free verified caller ID, free optional robocall blocking, and damages enforceable by the people harmed, paid for by the phone companies that profit from carrying robocall traffic. The main costs fall on telecom providers, who would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from add-on blocking services. The risks are real but addressed: over-blocking could screen out legitimate calls (from doctors, schools, domestic violence shelters), so the bill built in exemptions, a whitelist for essential services, and an appeals process. No consumer-side drawback comparable to the nuisance and fraud it would stop.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee after referral in April 2018 and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 18, 2018 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken: it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill carried 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and was sponsored by Rep. Jackie Speier.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone companies avoided free mandated call-verification and blocking; scam robocallers kept operating. Consumers got nothing from this bill, though Congress passed related robocall legislation (the TRACED Act) the following year.

for.name: 17 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (all Democrats, including Reps. Norton, Tsongas, Cohen, Sherman, Huffman, Brownley, Grijalva, Velazquez)

against.name: Telecommunications industry
against.what_they_did: Carriers opposed mandated free call-blocking and caller-ID verification, which they preferred to sell as paid add-on services; this position was widely reported during the robocall debates.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 18, 2018 and never reported the bill out or scheduled it for action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors in the record, and it never advanced beyond a Democratic sponsor's referral to committee.

industries.note: Carriers would have had to deploy call-verification and blocking technology for every subscriber at no extra charge, absorb compliance costs, and face private suits and state actions for noncompliance. They also lose revenue from selling call-blocking as a premium add-on.
The bill targets operators whose business model depends on spoofed caller ID and mass autodialed calls, including foreign-originated scammers the do-not-call registry cannot reach.
